title: History: acute right iliac fossa pain

header.contentArea: History taking — acute abdominal pain (right iliac fossa)
guidelineVersions: WSES Jerusalem Guidelines, 2025 edition (published online 28 Jan 2026)

related.why: Shares acute-abdomen safety-netting and escalation language

brief.role: You are the core surgical trainee on the general surgical take.
brief.scenario: A 23-year-old woman has been referred with a 14-hour history of abdominal pain, now settled in the right iliac fossa.
brief.task: Take a focused history. You do not need to examine the patient. At the end, summarise your findings and give a working differential to the examiner.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: This is a focused pain history plus the two questions that change management: migration, and pregnancy status.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Anchoring on appendicitis early and skipping the pregnancy question in a woman of reproductive age.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Ask her to describe the pain in her own words before you structure it.

flow: Characterise the pain and its migration
Take a targeted gynaecological, urinary and background history
Summarise back and state your differential

grid.label: Structures the pain history
grid.fail: Asks closed, disorganised questions and misses site, onset or character.
grid.pass: Covers site, onset, character, radiation, aggravating factors and associated symptoms in a structured way.
grid.high: Structures fluently, and lets the patient's own words shape the follow-up questions rather than working from a checklist.

grid.label: Elicits pain migration
grid.fail: Does not ask whether the pain started elsewhere or has moved.
grid.pass: Establishes that the pain began peri-umbilically before localising to the right iliac fossa.
grid.high: Elicits the migration and, when summarising, explicitly links it to visceral pain being replaced by parietal peritoneal irritation.

grid.label: Screens the core associated symptoms
grid.fail: Omits anorexia, nausea/vomiting and fever, or asks only after being prompted.
grid.pass: Asks about anorexia, nausea or vomiting, and fever or rigors.
grid.high: Asks about anorexia, nausea/vomiting and fever, and establishes that vomiting followed the pain rather than preceding it.

grid.label: Excludes pregnancy and a gynaecological cause
grid.fail: Does not ask about last menstrual period or the possibility of pregnancy in a woman of reproductive age.
grid.pass: Asks LMP and the possibility of pregnancy, and states a urine pregnancy test is needed before any imaging or treatment decision.
grid.high: Asks LMP, contraception and discharge, and tells the examiner that ectopic pregnancy must be actively excluded in any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain, regardless of stated risk factors.

grid.label: Takes a focused urinary and bowel history
grid.fail: Does not screen for urinary symptoms or a change in bowel habit.
grid.pass: Asks about dysuria, frequency, and any change in bowel habit or diarrhoea.
grid.high: Uses the urinary and bowel screen to actively argue against mimics such as UTI, gastroenteritis or mesenteric adenitis when summarising.

grid.label: Takes background history relevant to the differential
grid.fail: Does not ask about previous abdominal or gynaecological surgery, or previous similar episodes.
grid.pass: Asks about previous abdominal surgery, relevant past medical history and any previous similar episodes.
grid.high: Uses the surgical and gynaecological history to actively reconsider the differential rather than asking it as a checklist item.

grid.label: Summarises and presents a working differential
grid.fail: Gives no summary, or one the patient or examiner cannot follow.
grid.pass: Summarises the history in plain language and states a working diagnosis of probable appendicitis.
grid.high: Summarises fluently, offers a structured differential (appendicitis, ovarian pathology, ectopic pregnancy, UTI, mesenteric adenitis) and states the immediate next step.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: So, what's brought you in today?

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: I've got this pain in my tummy, it's been there since yesterday.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Okay. Is it sharp or dull? Is it constant?

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: It's sharp now, it's in my right side.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: I was sick once this morning.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Right, and how's your appetite been?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Okay, thank you. I think this sounds like appendicitis.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hi, I'm one of the surgical doctors. Can you tell me, in your own words, what's brought you in?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: I've had this pain in my tummy since yesterday evening, it's now mostly on my right side.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Okay. Whereabouts did it start, and has it moved anywhere?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: It started around my belly button, then a few hours later it moved down to the right.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: And what's the pain like now — sharp or dull, constant or coming and going?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Constant and sharp, worse if I move or cough.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Have you felt sick, gone off your food, or had any fevers or chills?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: I've been off my food and felt sick, vomited once. No fevers that I've noticed.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Any burning passing urine, or any change in your bowel habit?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: No, waterworks are fine, bowels are normal.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: When was your last period, and is there any chance you could be pregnant?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: About two weeks ago, and no, I don't think so.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Thank you — I'll still arrange a urine pregnancy test, that's routine for anyone of childbearing age with this kind of pain.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Have you had any tummy surgery before, or had anything like this happen previously?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: No surgery, and no, this is new.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: So to summarise: pain that started around your belly button and moved to the right, with loss of appetite and one episode of vomiting, no urinary or bowel symptoms, and no previous surgery. This is most consistent with appendicitis, though I'll examine you and check a pregnancy test and bloods to be sure.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello, I'm one of the surgical doctors. Could you tell me, in your own words, what's brought you in today?

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: I've had pain in my tummy since yesterday evening, it's settled on my right side now.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Can you point to exactly where it is, and tell me whereabouts it started?

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: It started around my belly button and moved down here to the right over about six hours.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That migration from around the belly button to the right lower side is a useful clue. Is it sharp, dull or constant, and does anything make it worse?

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Sharp and constant, worse with movement, coughing and the car journey here.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Pain that's worse on movement and coughing suggests irritation of the lining of the tummy, which fits appendicitis. Have you lost your appetite, felt sick, vomited, or had any fevers or shivering?

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Off my food, felt sick, vomited once after the pain started. No fevers I've noticed.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Good — vomiting after the pain, rather than before, also fits better with appendicitis than a stomach bug. Any burning or frequency passing urine, or any change in your bowel habit or diarrhoea?

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: No urinary symptoms, bowels normal, no diarrhoea.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That helps rule out a water infection or a stomach bug as the main cause. When was the first day of your last period, and is there any chance you could be pregnant?

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: About two weeks ago, and I really don't think I'm pregnant.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'll still send a urine pregnancy test before we go further — in any woman of your age with this kind of pain, we actively exclude an ectopic pregnancy even without risk factors, because it can otherwise be missed.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Have you ever had abdominal or gynaecological surgery, or anything similar to this before?

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: No surgery, and nothing like this before.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: So to summarise: a young woman with pain that migrated from the peri-umbilical region to the right iliac fossa over about six hours, worse on movement and coughing, with anorexia and a single episode of vomiting after the pain started, no urinary, bowel or gynaecological red flags, and no relevant past history. My leading diagnosis is acute appendicitis. My differential also includes ovarian pathology and ectopic pregnancy, which I'll exclude with a pregnancy test, and I'd like to examine her and send routine bloods.

failures.move: Does not ask whether the pain started elsewhere before localising.
failures.consequence: Misses the classic migratory pattern that separates appendicitis from other causes of right iliac fossa pain, weakening the differential offered.

failures.move: Skips LMP and pregnancy questions in a woman of reproductive age.
failures.consequence: Risks missing a life-threatening ectopic pregnancy; this is treated as a patient-safety failure regardless of how well the rest of the history is taken.

failures.move: Does not ask about urinary or bowel symptoms.
failures.consequence: Leaves UTI and gastrointestinal mimics unexplored, so the differential presented to the examiner is incomplete.

failures.move: Does not ask about previous abdominal or gynaecological surgery.
failures.consequence: Misses information that would materially change the differential, such as a previous appendicectomy.

recovery.when: You realise partway through that you've forgotten to ask about migration.
recovery.line: Can I just go back — where exactly did the pain start, before it settled here?

recovery.when: The patient asks if she is definitely pregnant before your test result is back.
recovery.line: I can't say for certain until the test result is back, but I'm arranging it now as routine for anyone in your situation.

knowledge.fact: Classic appendicitis pain starts peri-umbilically before localising to the right iliac fossa, as visceral pain from appendiceal obstruction is replaced by parietal peritoneal irritation.
Anorexia, nausea and vomiting typically follow the onset of pain in appendicitis; vomiting that clearly precedes the pain points away from the diagnosis.
About a third of women with an ectopic pregnancy have no known risk factors, so exclude pregnancy in every woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain (NICE NG126, rec 1.3.8).

Right iliac fossa pain in a woman of reproductive age always needs a gynaecological differential considered alongside appendicitis, including ovarian cyst accident, torsion and pelvic inflammatory disease.
A low score on a clinical scoring system such as Alvarado supports, but does not replace, clinical judgement, and does not on its own exclude appendicitis.

recall.think: A missed ectopic pregnancy or a perforating appendix.
recall.say: This sounds most consistent with acute appendicitis; I want to exclude an ectopic pregnancy first.
do: Ask LMP; send a pregnancy test

numbers.meaning: of women with an ectopic pregnancy have no known risk factors

recall.trap: Anchoring on appendicitis and skipping the pregnancy question.
recall.finish: Examine, pregnancy test and bloods, discuss with the registrar.

partner.opening: You are a 23-year-old woman with a 14-hour history of pain that started around the belly button and has now settled in the right iliac fossa. Give information naturally, only when asked the right question.
partner.actorBrief: Give information only when the candidate asks the specific question. If asked an open question, give a brief general answer and wait for follow-up. Play mild discomfort, not distress.

reveals.trigger: asks where the pain started or whether it has moved
reveals.finding: Pain started around the belly button yesterday evening and moved to the right lower tummy about six hours later.

reveals.trigger: asks about vomiting, appetite or fever
reveals.finding: Off food since yesterday, vomited once after the pain started, no fevers noticed.

reveals.trigger: asks about urinary or bowel symptoms
reveals.finding: No urinary symptoms, bowels normal, no diarrhoea.

reveals.trigger: asks about last period or the possibility of pregnancy
reveals.finding: Last period about two weeks ago; doesn't think she's pregnant but has no strong reason to be certain.

reveals.trigger: asks about previous abdominal or gynaecological surgery, or similar episodes
reveals.finding: No previous surgery, and nothing like this has happened before.

push.question: What do you think might be wrong with me?
push.expect: A clear, jargon-light explanation naming appendicitis as the leading diagnosis without over-promising certainty.

push.question: Could I be pregnant even though my test is negative?
push.expect: Explains a negative urine test lowers but does not fully exclude pregnancy at very early gestation, and that ongoing pain still needs reassessment.

push.question: Do I definitely need an operation?
push.expect: Explains the diagnosis needs confirming first (examination, bloods, possibly imaging) before any decision about surgery.

curveballs.prompt: Actually, I forgot — I'm on the combined pill, does that change anything?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Explains this doesn't remove the need for a pregnancy test, and notes it as part of the contraceptive and gynaecological history.

curveballs.prompt: My mum had bowel cancer at 45 — should I be worried it's that?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Acknowledges the concern, notes this is an acute presentation unlike a cancer history, and says it will be flagged and discussed appropriately without dismissing it.

curveballs.prompt: The pain's actually got a lot worse just now, is that normal?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Takes it seriously, asks about the change directly, and says the team needs to reassess urgently rather than continuing routine questions.
